text.p: Sears, Roebuck and Co said Thurday it had estimated its costs for settling claims related to illegal collections of credit card debt would be between $178 million and $265 million.

Earlier, Sears said it had reached settlements with state regulators and consumers in four class action lawsuits over the way it collected payments from Sears credit card customers who filed for bankruptcy between 1992 and 1997.
Sears Chairman and Chief Executive Arthur Martinez said the company's collection efforts were illegal and the affair had damaged the reputation of the nation's No. 2 retailer.

"We clearly were not behaving appropriately," Martinez said during a call with reporters. "We're not selling products that kill people. But in this case we were collecting money improperly and illegally, and there's no way to not to call that a black eye."
Sears will take a charge in the second quarter to cover the settlement costs, he said. But the company did not reveal the size of the charge because the cost to resolve the case still could change.

In the accords announced Thursday, Sears agreed to pay between $90 million and $160 million to credit card customers who signed repayment agreements with Sears, which was required by law to file the agreements in bankruptcy court but did not.

Sears pledged an additional $23 million to $40 million, representing 10 percent interest on amounts illegally collected. It also agreed to pay $25 million in penalties and $40 million for a pool to fund consumer education.
The total cost to Sears could swing wildly, depending on how many consumers qualify for payment.

The retailer has launched a record search to determine how many customers apply for repayment since 1992. Still, the settlement is designed to cover cases dating back to 1979, although Sears said identifying claims between 1992 and 1979 will be difficult because its records are not reliable.
In addition, Sears was negotiating with the U.S. Justice Department, which could impose sanctions on the retailer, Sears said.

Under the settlements, Sears gave up its right to reclaim merchandise that consumers did not pay for. The company anticipates taking a write-off of an undisclosed amount for waiving its security interest in those goods, Martinez said.
"The one thing we can hold our head up about here is that we moved forward aggressively, we moved forward quickly to resolve it," Martinez said.
